newsitem.title: LATVIA: Finland, Latvia want Russia in security system.
newsitem.headline: Finland, Latvia want Russia in security system.

text.p: The Baltic state of Latvia and Finland said on Monday they favoured tying their neighbour Russia more closely into a new European security system.
Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen, on a one-day visit to Latvia, said Russia should not be left out as Western planners set their sights on a new post-Cold War security framework.
"There is a need for a more complex European security system, where Russia is better integrated," Lipponen told a news conference.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation says it is ready to open its ranks to some at least of Moscow's former satellites in the old communist bloc.
But Russia says NATO expansion would create new dividing lines in Europe and opposes efforts to include its former Cold War allies in the alliance.
Finland has a cautious policy on NATO, saying it does not want to join but respects the choice of others to sign up.
Lipponen said the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) could boost security but NATO should increase ties with Russia.
The OSCE, meeting on Monday in Lisbon, monitors minority rights and aims to reduce conflicts among nations.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in Lisbon set out a vision where the OSCE would play a larger security role and keep all countries in Europe on an even footing.
But Russia has little support for turning the OSCE into a counterbalance to NATO.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Shkele also said he favoured stronger ties between NATO and Russia although any agreements should be made in the open.
"Latvia would be in favour of both NATO and Russia signing an agreement but with its contents sufficiently well-known to countries in the region," Shkele said.

Shkele reiterated the position of all three Baltic states -- Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia -- that the protection of NATO is the only way to avoid repeating a history where they have been invaded and occupied by more powerful neighbours.
